title: The young monk (373–382)
hookLine: rouse yourself by yourself; a young monk who applies himself lights up the world like the moon
last: PAÑÑĀ — ONE BUCKET AT A TIME.

cards: A kid practicing free throws in the driveway after dark. A cook who tastes the soup six times. A teenager learning a language on their own, just because they love it.
You've probably met someone like that, doing one thing with their whole heart. There's a brightness about them; you notice it across a room. Nobody told them to.
They roused themselves. The mendicant chapter ends with exactly that picture: someone young, wholehearted, and shining.

teach.b: The last verses of chapter twenty-five read like advice to a new monk. Go into an empty room and sit with a quiet heart, seeing the teaching clearly, and there's a joy beyond ordinary joys.
Watching the body's pieces arise and pass away brings happiness, the text says. Guard the senses, be content, keep good friends.
Then a lovely picture: as the jasmine drops its withered flowers, drop greed and hatred. Then the heart of the passage.
Rouse yourself by yourself; examine yourself by yourself. You are your own protector, and your own refuge. Train yourself the way a merchant trains a good horse.

teach.h: LIKE THE MOON FREE FROM CLOUDS.
teach.b: And the chapter's last verse, three hundred eighty-two, in Max Müller's English: "He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds."
The commentary connects it to a novice named Sumana, still a child, whom the Buddha praised. The point isn't age. You don't have to wait until you're wise, or old, or finished, to shine.
You shine by applying yourself, now.

This week followed thirst and its way out: the creeper of tanha and digging up its root, the web you spun and stepping out of it, the best gift, the teaching, bhikkhu and restraint of the senses, the emptied boat.
Now a young monk lights up the world, and tomorrow the last chapter begins.

how: In several Buddhist countries children may ordain as novices, sometimes for a few weeks or a season; teachers use verse 382 to encourage the young, and verses 379–380 to teach self-reliance in practice.

o: an elder monk honored for long years in robes
young, like a new monk who shines by effort
a wandering hermit who lives alone in a forest

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: brightens the world like the moon
a child novice in the commentary

s: verse 382 says you must be old to shine
it praises a young monk who applies himself: brightness comes from effort, not age.
the verses call you your own protector and refuge
rouse yourself by yourself; examine yourself by yourself.
the jasmine image is about keeping every flower
as the jasmine drops its withered flowers, drop greed and hatred.

games.q: you're new to a practice and surrounded by people who've done it for decades. what do today's verses suggest?
o: wait until you're experienced to take it seriously.
games.why: verse 382: even a young monk who applies himself brightens up the world like the moon when free from clouds.

practice: For this sit, do one thing wholeheartedly: breathe, giving each breath your whole attention the way the kid gives it to the free throw, as it begins, fills, turns and leaves.
When the mind wanders, rouse yourself, by yourself, with no scolding, and come back to the next breath fresh, like a beginner. You are the young monk here.

wordCard.voice: Dahara. Young: rouse yourself by yourself, since whoever applies themselves wholeheartedly, even young, brightens the world like the moon out of the clouds.

orig.note: Pali dahara: young; verse 382 speaks of the 'daharo bhikkhu', the young monk.

carryVoice: Your line: young and awake. You don't have to wait to shine. Day two hundred twenty-four, done.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: He who, even as a young Bhikshu, applies himself to the doctrine of Buddha, brightens up this world, like the moon when free from clouds.
